relationships.description: The throttling policy is advertised to clients through a response header, such as X-RateLimit-Remaining or Retry-After, that reports the consumer's remaining quota, window reset time or back-off interval.
relationships.evidence: The rate-limit extension in the OpenAPI document names the header, and the corresponding Response headers map declares that same X-RateLimit-* or Retry-After header.

relationships.description: The throttling policy derives its counting key from the credential presented under a security scheme, so the API key, bearer token subject or OAuth client ID identifies whose requests are counted.
relationships.evidence: The rate-limit key configuration (for example key: header:X-API-Key or key: jwt.sub) refers to the credential defined by the security scheme under components.securitySchemes.

relationships.description: The throttling policy sets the request quota and window that a specific method-path operation must honor, and it determines when calls to that operation are rejected.
relationships.evidence: The operation carries an x-ratelimit extension or references the policy, or a gateway policy file or throttle decorator on the route handler binds the limit to that method and path.

relationships.description: The throttling policy is the concrete API configuration that puts a recorded abuse-prevention or denial-of-service countermeasure into effect.
relationships.evidence: The threat model or security register lists the countermeasure, such as brute-force or DoS throttling, with its implementation pointing to this rate-limit definition or the gateway configuration that deploys it.

relationships.description: The throttling policy keeps API usage within a stated restriction, such as a contractual tier quota, an upstream provider's usage cap or a cost ceiling, by enforcing a matching request cap.
relationships.evidence: A decision record, SLA or contract clause states the usage limit, and the rate-limit's requests-per-window value is traced to or derived from that clause.

relationships.description: The throttling policy is applied in front of an operation as a shared protective service that meters every invocation of that method-path pair before the handler runs.
relationships.evidence: The gateway or middleware configuration attaches the limiter to the operation's route, for example a Kong rate-limiting plugin scoped to that route or a throttle middleware registered on the handler.

relationships.description: The throttling policy applies across all methods under one URL path template and meters their combined traffic against a shared quota.
relationships.evidence: The path item carries the rate-limit extension, or the gateway configuration scopes a limiter to the path pattern with no method qualifier.

relationships.description: A narrower throttling policy, such as a premium-tier or per-operation override, inherits the counting key and enforcement behavior of a broader base policy and changes only some parameters, such as the quota or window.
relationships.evidence: The rate-limit definition declares an extends or base reference to another named policy, or a tier configuration overrides selected fields of a default limit.

relationships.description: Exceeding the throttling policy's quota causes the API to return a designated rejection response, typically HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.
relationships.evidence: The operation's responses map declares a 429 (or 503) response tied to the limit, and the limiter middleware or gateway is configured to emit that status when the quota is exhausted.

relationships.description: The throttling policy is enforced through platform software, such as an API gateway, reverse proxy or Redis cache, that stores the request counters and applies the cap at runtime.
relationships.evidence: The gateway, NGINX or Envoy configuration contains the limit_req or rate-limit filter for this policy, or the limiter library is configured with a Redis connection string for its counter store.

notes: governs.api.operation and serves.api.operation overlap; both attach a limit to an operation. 'governs' fits the semantics better. 'serves' toward an operation or path item inverts the usual meaning: a rate limit restricts rather than provides functionality. Consider merging into governs/constrains.
